Know Where You Stand: Stage, Customers and Business Model

You start by diagnosing your business honestly: which stage it is in, what is holding it back, who really buys and why, and how all the parts fit on one page. These three lessons give you the evidence you need before you spend money on growth.
Survival, stable or ready to grow: diagnosing your business stage
Place your business in one of three stages using simple signs
Calculate your monthly profit and your profit per working hour
Identify the single biggest limit on your growth: demand, capacity, cash or time
Name the barriers women owners often face and one way to reduce each

Many women in Nigeria already run a business: a food stall, a tailoring shop, a hair salon, a poultry pen, a small provisions store. This course is for you if you are already selling and want the business to become stronger, more organised and more profitable. We will not start from zero. We will start by looking honestly at where your business stands today.
Three stages of a small business

Business advisers often describe small firms in stages. The names vary, but the idea is simple. At the **survival** stage, money comes in and goes out the same day, and the owner is not sure whether she made a profit. At the **stable** stage, sales are fairly regular, the owner knows her main costs and the business pays her something every month. At the **growth-ready** stage, the business is stable, demand is bigger than what she can currently supply, and she has the records to prove it. Growth spent at the wrong stage often fails: a loan taken at survival stage usually feeds the household, not the business.
Build each stage on the one below
Growth-ready: proven extra demand
Stable: regular sales, known costs
Survival: daily cash, no records
You cannot safely skip a level: growth sits on top of stability, and stability sits on records.

Find your real profit and your profit per hour

Profit is what is left after **all** business costs, not the money in your hand at the end of the day. To judge your stage, add up one month of sales, subtract one month of costs, then divide the profit by the hours you worked. Profit per hour tells you whether the business is paying you fairly for your time, which matters a great deal for women who also carry most of the cooking, childcare and caring at home.
Worked example: Aisha's small chops business
For example, Aisha makes puff-puff, samosa and spring rolls for parties in Kaduna. She wrote down every sale and cost for four weeks. Figures are illustrative and prices are approximate.
Monthly costs (flour, oil, fillings, packs, gas, transport): ₦128,000.
Hours worked on the business, counted from her diary: 70 hours.
Profit per hour: ₦63,000 divided by 70 = ₦900 per hour.
She also noticed she refused 3 party orders because her single fryer could not cook fast enough.

Aisha is stable: she knows her numbers and makes a profit. Her limit is capacity (one fryer), not demand, because customers are already asking for more than she can make. That points to a very different growth move from someone whose limit is too few customers.
What is really holding you back?
**Demand**: not enough people buying. Fix with customer research and better selling (Lesson 1.2).
**Capacity**: you cannot make or deliver more. Fix with equipment, a helper or a better process (Module 3).
**Cash**: you cannot buy stock or inputs in advance. Fix with deposits, tighter credit and planned funding (Lessons 2.1 and 3.1).
**Time**: you are the bottleneck for every task. Fix with delegation and routines (Lesson 3.2).

Customer discovery: interviewing real buyers and writing a customer profile
Plan 10 to 15 short customer conversations
Ask questions about past behaviour instead of opinions
Tally answers to find patterns you can trust
Write a one-paragraph customer profile with evidence

Most owners describe their customers as "everybody". In practice, a small group of people brings most of your money, and they buy for specific reasons. **Customer discovery** means talking to real buyers to find out who they are, what problem you solve for them, and what makes them choose you or leave you. It costs almost nothing except your time.
Ask about the past, not the future

People are polite. If you ask "Would you buy my new product?" most will say yes and never buy. The book *The Mom Test* by Rob Fitzpatrick explains a better approach: ask about what people **actually did** recently, avoid pitching your idea, and listen for specific details such as dates, amounts and alternatives they used. Past behaviour is the best evidence of future behaviour.
Weak question (opinion)
Strong question (past behaviour)
Do you like my service?
The last time you used a laundry, what happened?
Would you pay ₦1,500 for this?
How much did you spend on this last month?
Is delivery important to you?
What did you do the last time your clothes came back late?
Would you recommend me?
Have you told anyone about us? What did you say?

Choose who to talk to

Discovery is a short, repeatable process, not a one-time survey.
Who to talk to
**Your best regular customers**: they tell you what you do well.
**Customers who stopped buying**: they tell you what went wrong.
**People who buy from a competitor**: they tell you what you are missing.
Aim for 10 to 15 conversations of about 10 minutes each, in person, on a call or by WhatsApp voice note.
Two people sitting and talking in a conversation
A short, respectful conversation with a real buyer beats any guess about the market.
Six questions that work
"Tell me about the last time you bought [this kind of product or service]."
"What was the hardest or most annoying part?"
"What did you do about it? Did you try anyone else?"
"Roughly how much do you spend on this in a month?"
"Why did you choose us, and what nearly made you choose someone else?"
"Who else do you know who has this problem?"
Respect people's data

Ask permission before you save someone's phone number or quote them. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 expects businesses to collect only the personal data they need, for a clear purpose, and to keep it secure. Do not share customers' numbers or screenshots of their chats with anyone.
Worked example: Blessing's laundry interviews

For example, Blessing runs a wash-and-iron service in Port Harcourt. Sales were flat, so she spoke to 12 people in two weeks: 7 regular customers, 2 who had stopped using her and 3 who used a dry-cleaner nearby.
She wrote short notes after each conversation and tallied repeated answers.
8 of the 12 worked in offices or banks and had no time to wash on weekdays: 8 ÷ 12 = 67 percent.
7 of the 12 said late return was their biggest frustration: 7 ÷ 12 = 58 percent.
Both former customers had left after clothes came back a day late before an important event.
Only 2 people mentioned price at all; the 3 dry-cleaner users already paid more than Blessing charges.
5 people said they would happily pay for pickup and drop-off at their office.

Blessing learned that her real customer is a busy office worker who values reliable timing more than a low price. Her growth idea changed from "cut prices" to "guarantee 48-hour return with office pickup".
Write your customer profile

A customer profile is a short paragraph, backed by your tally, that answers: **who** buys (age range, work, location), **what problem** they have, **what they used before**, **why they choose you**, **what would make them leave**, and **where you can reach** more people like them. Keep the numbers from your tally beside each claim so you can check it later.
How many conversations is enough?

You are not running a national survey. You are looking for patterns. After about 8 to 10 conversations with similar customers, answers usually start to repeat. If every conversation still tells you something completely new, your customers may be more varied than you thought, so keep going or split them into two groups, for example households and shops, and write a short profile for each.

Blessing's profile reads: "Office and bank staff aged about 25 to 45 in our area, with no time to wash on weekdays. Their main frustration is late return (7 of 12). They choose us because we are close and careful with fabrics. They leave when we miss a deadline. We can reach more of them through office receptionists and WhatsApp status." One paragraph like this guides your pricing, marketing and growth plan.
Ask about what people did, not what they think they might do.
Talk to best customers, lost customers and competitors' customers.
Tally answers; a pattern from 12 real people beats a guess.

Your one-page business model and an honest readiness check

Once you know your stage and your customer, you need a picture of the whole business on one page. The **Business Model Canvas**, created by Alexander Osterwalder and published by Strategyzer, is a widely used one-page tool for this. It has nine blocks. You can draw it on a sheet of paper in ten minutes.
Block
Question it answers
Customer Segments
Who are my most important customers?
Value Propositions
What problem do I solve or what need do I meet for them?
Channels
How do customers find me, buy and receive the product?
Customer Relationships
How do I keep them coming back?
Revenue Streams
What do they pay for, how much and how?
Key Resources
What equipment, skills, money or space do I need?
Key Activities
What must I do well every week?
Key Partnerships
Which suppliers or partners do I rely on?
Cost Structure
What are my biggest costs?
A person standing beside a large planning board
The canvas puts your whole business on one page so weak spots become visible.
Worked example: Titi's egg business canvas
For example, Titi keeps about 500 laying hens behind her house near Ibadan and sells crates of eggs. Her canvas, written in a notebook, looks like this.
Customer Segments: two bakeries, one hotel kitchen, about 20 households and 3 market retailers.
Value Propositions: fresh eggs delivered twice a week, consistent size, honest crate count.
Channels: WhatsApp orders, delivery by a hired keke, collection from her gate.
Customer Relationships: personal calls, a WhatsApp broadcast list, credit for the hotel.
Revenue Streams: crates of eggs, plus spent hens sold at the end of the laying cycle.
Key Resources: hens, pen, feeders and drinkers, her own knowledge, a helper.
Key Activities: feeding, cleaning, egg collection and grading, vaccinations, delivery.
Key Partnerships: feed supplier, a veterinary adviser, the keke rider.
Cost Structure: feed is by far the largest cost, then labour, vaccines and transport.
Two weak spots stand out. Almost all revenue depends on feed prices she cannot control, and the hotel's credit means her cash arrives late. These become her first things to fix.
The 20-point readiness check
Score each statement 0 (not true), 1 (partly true) or 2 (fully true). Be honest; nobody else needs to see it. A score shows where to start, not whether you are a good business owner.
Growth readiness checklist
Records kept for 3 months
Business money kept separate
Unit cost known per product
Customer profile written
Cash reserve for one month
Five of the ten checks; the full list is below and each scores 0, 1 or 2.
1. I have written records of sales and costs for at least three months.
2. Business money is kept separate from household money.
3. I know the full cost of each main product or service, including my time.
4. My prices cover my costs and leave a profit.
5. I have a written customer profile based on real conversations.
6. At least half of my sales come from repeat customers.
7. I have enough cash to run the business for one month if sales stop.
8. I know which registration or permits apply to me (CAC, NAFDAC, local levies).
9. Someone else can run key tasks for a day if I am away.
10. I have one written goal for the next three months.
Worked example: Titi's readiness score
For example, Titi scores her egg business honestly.
Fully true (2 points each): statements 1, 2 and 6 = 6 points.
Partly true (1 point each): statements 3, 4, 8, 9 and 10 = 5 points.
Not true (0 points): statements 5 and 7 = 0 points.
Total: 6 + 5 + 0 = 11 out of 20.

Titi's lowest areas are a missing customer profile and no cash reserve. She decides to interview her customers this month and to start setting aside part of each week's profit until she holds one month of feed money.
Read your score

Under 8: focus on records and separating money before anything else. 8 to 14: fix your two lowest items over the next month. 15 and above: you are probably ready to plan a growth move, which we cover in Module 3.
How the blocks connect

The canvas is useful because the blocks depend on each other. If you change one block, check the others. When Titi adds hotels as a customer segment, her channels change (she needs scheduled delivery), her customer relationships change (credit and invoices), her key activities change (grading eggs by size) and her cost structure changes (more transport). A change that looks small on one block can add costs elsewhere, so update the whole page before you decide.
Keep your canvas and score in one folder or one phone album. You will update both at the end of the course, and the change between the two versions becomes part of your final project.

Run It Well: Order Costing, Quality Standards and a Monthly Dashboard

This module turns good intentions into routines. You will cost and quote a full customer order, set quality and safety standards that others can follow, and track a small set of numbers every month so you can see real progress instead of guessing.
Costing and quoting a full order: inputs, your time, delivery and payment fees
List every cost line in a customer order, including your own time
Calculate a quote that protects a target profit margin
Include payment fees in the price instead of absorbing them
Set a deposit that covers what you must buy before the job

Growing businesses increasingly sell by **order**: a party tray, a set of uniforms, 30 crates of eggs for a hotel, a month of office laundry. An order has costs that a single item on a table does not show: delivery, extra packaging, a helper for the day, payment fees and, very often, your own long hours. If you quote from habit, a big order can make you busy and poorer at the same time.
The six cost lines of an order
**Direct inputs**: ingredients, fabric, feed, detergent: everything that goes into the product.
**Packaging**: packs, bags, labels, crates.
**Shared running costs**: the order's fair share of gas, electricity or fuel for a generator.
**Delivery**: transport to the customer, including the return trip.
**Labour**: helpers, plus **your own hours** at a fair rate (decide one, for example ₦1,000 per hour).
**Payment costs**: gateway or POS charges and transfer fees, usually a percentage of the price.
Building an order quote
Count direct inputs
Add packaging and shared costs
Add delivery and labour
Choose target margin
Allow for payment fees
Quote and take deposit
Each step adds a cost you can see, so nothing is forgotten when you name the price.
From cost to quote: the margin formula

**Margin** is profit as a share of the selling price. If you want a 25 percent margin, the cost must be 75 percent of the price. So: **price = total cost ÷ (1 minus target margin)**. If a payment fee is charged as a percentage of the price, subtract it too: **price = total cost ÷ (1 minus margin minus fee rate)**. Doing this protects your margin, because the fee grows with the price.
Worked example: Aisha quotes 50 party packs

For example, a client in Kaduna asks Aisha for 50 small chops packs for a birthday. The client will pay through a payment link. Prices are approximate and for illustration only; check your own supplier and gateway rates.
Ingredients (flour, oil, meat, vegetables, spices): ₦38,500.
Packaging: 50 packs × ₦250 = ₦12,500.
Gas share ₦4,000, delivery to the venue ₦5,000, one helper for the day ₦5,000.
Aisha's own time: 10 hours × ₦1,000 = ₦10,000.
Target margin 25 percent, payment link fee assumed at 1.5 percent: 75,000 ÷ (1 − 0.25 − 0.015) = 75,000 ÷ 0.735 = about ₦102,041.
She rounds to ₦2,050 per pack: 50 × ₦2,050 = ₦102,500.
Aisha quotes ₦102,500 for 50 packs. If she had quoted ₦1,800 per pack from habit (₦90,000), her profit after the fee would have been about ₦13,650, roughly half, for exactly the same work.

Delivery is a real cost of every order, so it belongs in the quote, not in your pocket.
Deposits protect your cash

For orders, ask for a deposit that at least covers what you must buy in advance. In Aisha's case, ingredients and packaging cost ₦51,000, so a 50 percent deposit of ₦51,250 covers them. Put your terms in writing, even in a WhatsApp message: the quantity, price, delivery date and time, deposit, when the balance is due, and what happens if the client cancels late.
Fake payment alerts

Never release goods because of an SMS or a screenshot. Confirm every payment inside your own bank or wallet app (for example your bank app, Opay or Moniepoint) before delivery. Scammers send convincing fake credit alerts, especially on large orders.
When the client asks for a discount
Quoting service work by time

If you sell a service such as tailoring, hair styling, cleaning or tutoring, most of the cost is time. Work out an **hourly cost** first: add your monthly fixed costs (rent, power, phone data, equipment repairs) and the pay you want for yourself, then divide by the hours you can really sell in a month. For example, ₦60,000 fixed costs plus ₦90,000 owner pay = ₦150,000; divided by 100 sellable hours, that is ₦1,500 an hour. A job that takes 4 hours with ₦2,000 of materials costs 4 × ₦1,500 + ₦2,000 = ₦8,000 before profit and fees.

Before you agree, work out what the discount does to your profit. A 10 percent discount on ₦102,500 is ₦10,250, which removes about 40 percent of Aisha's ₦25,962 profit. Offer something that costs you less instead: free delivery when the client collects nearby, or a smaller pack size at a lower total. Payment fees and gateway rates change, so check your provider's current price list every few months.
An order has six cost lines; your own time and payment fees are the ones most often forgotten.
Price = total cost ÷ (1 − target margin − fee rate) protects your margin.

Confirm payments in your own app, never by SMS or screenshot.

Quality standards, safety and fair treatment as you grow
Write a simple quality standard that a helper can follow
Measure your complaint rate and use a complaint log
Apply core safety practices for food, heat, electricity and money
Treat customers and workers fairly and protect their data

When you do everything yourself, quality lives in your hands and your head. As soon as a helper joins, or orders double, quality depends on whether your standard is **written down** and **checked**. Customers forgive a small business many things, but not unreliable quality. In Lesson 1.2, Blessing learned that late return was the main reason customers left her laundry.
Write a one-page quality standard
List the steps of your main product or service in order.
For each step, write what "good" looks like in a way anyone can check: a time, a weight, a count, a photo.
Mark the two or three steps where mistakes cost the most.
Add a final check before anything leaves your hands.
Train your helper with the sheet, then watch them do it once.
Quality without and with a written standard
Without a standard
With a standard
Quality depends on mood
Helper guesses what you want
Complaints repeat
Owner checks everything herself
Same result every time
Helper follows the sheet
Complaints logged and fixed
Owner checks only key steps
A written standard lets quality survive when you are not standing beside the work.
Track your complaint rate

Keep a **complaint log**: date, customer, what went wrong, what you did, and the cause. Then calculate the **complaint rate**: complaints divided by orders or items, times 100. A number lets you see whether a change really worked.
Worked example: Blessing's laundry standard

For example, Blessing logged complaints for a month, then introduced a written standard: every bag tagged with the customer's name and promised return date, a fabric check before washing, and a count of items on drop-off and on return.
Month 1: 240 items processed, 6 complaints. Rate = 6 ÷ 240 × 100 = 2.5 percent.
Four of the six were late returns and two were missing items.
Month 2 (with the standard): 300 items, 3 complaints. Rate = 3 ÷ 300 × 100 = 1 percent.
No item went missing in Month 2 because items were counted in and out.
Blessing's complaint rate fell from 2.5 percent to 1 percent while volume rose by 60 items. The written standard, not extra effort from Blessing, made the difference.
A person ticking items on a large checklist
A short written checklist keeps quality steady as your team and orders grow.
Safety basics for a growing business
Area
Recognised practice
Food
Follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, use safe water and raw materials.
Gas and heat
Cook in a ventilated space, check hoses and regulators for leaks with soapy water, keep a fire blanket or extinguisher nearby, and never leave hot oil unattended.
Electricity
Do not overload sockets, keep irons and appliances away from water, unplug when not in use, and site generators outdoors away from doors and windows because exhaust fumes can kill.
Confirm payments in your own app, never share OTPs or PINs, and bank cash daily instead of keeping large amounts at the shop.
Products
If you make food, drinks or cosmetics for sale, check what NAFDAC registration applies before scaling up.
Generators

Carbon monoxide from generator exhaust has no smell and can kill people sleeping or working nearby. Always run a generator outside, well away from doors, windows and vents, and never inside a shop, kitchen or house.
Inclusion and fairness
**Workers**: agree pay, hours and tasks in writing, pay on the agreed day, and give helpers safe working conditions.

**Customers**: treat every customer with respect, make your service usable for older customers and people with disabilities (for example, delivery or a phone order option), and give clear prices up front.
**Data**: under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, collect only the customer data you need, ask consent for marketing messages, and keep records secure.
**Opportunity**: when you hire, give fair consideration to women and young people in your community who need the work.
Handling a complaint well
Listen fully without interrupting or defending yourself.
Thank the customer for telling you; many unhappy customers simply leave without a word.
Agree a fair fix quickly: redo the job, replace the item or refund part of the price.
Write the complaint and its cause in your log the same day.
Change the standard or the training so the same problem does not repeat.
A complaint handled quickly and fairly often turns a customer into a loyal one, because it proves you care about getting things right.

Check your standard every few months. When you change a supplier, add a new product or hire a new helper, walk through the sheet again and update any step that no longer matches how the work is really done. An out-of-date standard is ignored quickly, so keep it short, current and pinned where the work happens.
Quality, safety and fairness are not extras for later. They are what make customers trust you with bigger orders, and what make good helpers stay.
Write your quality standard so a helper can follow and check it.
Complaint rate = complaints ÷ orders × 100; track it monthly.
Use recognised safety practice for food, gas, electricity and money.
Fair pay, respectful service and careful data handling build trust.

Decide one action
Act and record
The same review every month turns records into decisions.
Worked example: Titi's three-month dashboard

For example, Titi tracks her egg business. Prices are approximate and for illustration: she sells at about ₦5,500 per crate, direct costs (mainly feed) are about ₦4,200 per crate, and fixed costs (helper, vaccines, transport, levies) are about ₦90,000 a month.
Crates sold: Month 1 = 120, Month 2 = 135, Month 3 = 150.
Gross profit per crate: 5,500 − 4,200 = ₦1,300. Gross margin = 1,300 ÷ 5,500 × 100 = about 23.6 percent.
Net profit after ₦90,000 fixed costs: ₦66,000, ₦85,500, ₦105,000.
But in Month 3 the hotel still owes ₦180,000 for eggs delivered on credit, so her cash fell even though profit rose.
Repeat customers in Month 3: 18 of 24 customers bought again = 75 percent.

Titi's business is growing and profitable, but cash is the warning sign. Her one action for next month: agree with the hotel to pay every two weeks instead of monthly, and stop new credit above an agreed limit.
A person reviewing progress bars on a board
Writing the same six numbers each month shows you the trend before it becomes a crisis.
Why profit and cash can differ

Profit counts sales when you make them. Cash counts money when it actually arrives. If customers buy on credit, if you pay suppliers in advance, or if you buy equipment, your cash can fall while profit rises. Many profitable small businesses close because they run out of cash. Watching both numbers side by side is the protection.
Simple tools for your dashboard
A notebook page with six rows and one column per month works perfectly.
Google Sheets on your phone can add up the numbers and draw a chart for you.
If you sell through Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint, download the monthly transaction history to check your revenue figure.
Keep receipts for big costs in one envelope or phone album so you can check costs too.
One action, not ten

At each monthly review, choose only one action based on the weakest number. Write it at the bottom of the dashboard and check it next month. Small, repeated improvements add up faster than big plans that never start.
Warning signs on a dashboard
Revenue rising but gross margin falling: input costs have gone up and your prices have not followed.
Net profit flat while revenue grows: fixed costs are growing too fast, or discounts are eating profit.
Repeat customer rate falling: check your complaint log; quality or reliability may be slipping.
Cash below one month of running costs: slow down spending and collect debts before anything else.
Owner hours rising every month: plan a handover before you burn out.

Compare each month with the month before and with the same month last year if you have it, because festive seasons, school fees periods and the rainy season change sales for many businesses. A fall in January after a busy December is normal; a fall that continues for three months is a signal to act.

Mark any estimate with a small letter E beside it. Estimates are acceptable at the start, but each month try to replace one estimate with a recorded figure. Within a few months your dashboard will rest on real records, and you will trust it enough to make decisions from it.

Track your owner hours too. If revenue rises but your hours rise faster, growth is being paid for with your rest and family time. That is a sign to look at delegation, which you will plan in Lesson 3.2.
Track six numbers monthly: revenue, gross margin, net profit, cash, repeat rate and owner hours.
Gross margin shows what each sale contributes; net profit shows what the business earned.
Credit sales can make cash fall while profit rises.
End every review with one written action.

Grow With Discipline: Funding, Partnerships and Your 90-Day Plan

Now you turn your evidence into action. You will compare growth options and fund the best one safely, build partnerships and hand over tasks so the business no longer depends on you for everything, and finish with a 90-day growth plan that becomes your final project.
Choosing your next growth move and funding it safely
Compare growth options by effort and profit impact
Calculate the payback period of an investment
Test whether a loan repayment is affordable, including a bad-month scenario
Choose the safest funding source from savings, groups, cooperatives and lenders

Growth does not always mean a bigger shop or a big loan. It means more profit from a business that still runs well. Your diagnosis from Module 1 tells you your main limit; your dashboard from Module 2 tells you which numbers are weak. Now you choose **one** growth move that fixes the limit.
Five common growth moves
**Sell more to existing customers**: bigger packs, regular subscriptions, reminders before festive seasons.
**Reach new customers like your best ones**: use your customer profile to find more of the same people.
**Raise the price** where your quality and reliability justify it.
**Add capacity**: equipment, a helper or a better process so you can say yes to more orders.
**Add a product or service** that the same customers already ask for.
Effort versus profit impact
Quick wins: do first
Big bets: plan carefully
Small fixes: fit in
Avoid for now
Effort and cost (low to high)
Profit impact (high at top)
Start with high-impact, low-effort moves; plan big bets only with numbers.

Many owners jump to a big bet, such as a second shop, before trying the quick wins, such as asking each regular customer for a weekly standing order. Score each idea: how much extra monthly profit might it bring, and how much money and effort will it take?
Payback period

For any investment, calculate the **payback period**: cost of the investment ÷ extra monthly profit it brings. A short payback (a few months) is lower risk. A payback of several years for a small business is high risk, because things change.
Worked example: Aisha's second fryer

For example, in Lesson 1.1 Aisha found she refused about 3 orders a month because of her single fryer. A second fryer and gas burner would cost about ₦180,000 (approximate). Each extra order brings about ₦20,000 profit after all costs.
Extra monthly profit: 3 orders × ₦20,000 = ₦60,000.
Payback period: ₦180,000 ÷ ₦60,000 = 3 months.
Option A, save first: putting aside ₦30,000 a month, she can buy it in 6 months with no debt.
Option B, a loan of ₦180,000 repaid at ₦36,000 a month for 6 months: total repaid ₦216,000, so the loan costs ₦36,000.
Affordability: ₦60,000 extra profit − ₦36,000 repayment = ₦24,000 a month left over.
Bad-month test: if only 2 extra orders come, extra profit is ₦40,000 and only ₦4,000 is left after repayment.

The loan is affordable only if the extra orders are reliable. Aisha chooses a middle path: she uses a cooperative loan for half the cost and her savings for the rest, so her monthly repayment is smaller and a slow month will not break her.

Loan and grant scams

Genuine grants do not ask you to pay a "processing fee" to an individual's account. Raising your price as a growth move

A price increase can be the quickest win, because it needs no new equipment. If Titi raises her price from ₦5,500 to ₦5,800 per crate while costs stay the same, her gross profit per crate rises from ₦1,300 to ₦1,600. At 150 crates a month that is ₦45,000 more profit, even if she sells nothing extra. Give regular customers notice, explain the reason simply (for example, higher feed costs), and keep your quality steady.

Before signing any loan, ask the lender to write down the amount you receive, every fee, the total you will repay and the repayment dates. Compare the monthly repayment with the **extra** profit the loan will create, not with your total sales. Keep at least one month of running costs aside so a slow month does not force you to borrow again.

Partnerships, delegation and building your support network
Decide which tasks to hand to a helper and calculate whether it pays

A business that depends on the owner for every task cannot grow far, and the owner pays with her health and family time. Growth needs two kinds of help: **people who do tasks** for you and **partners who open doors**, such as suppliers, referrers, cooperatives and mentors.
What to delegate first

Delegate tasks that are repeatable, easy to check and take a lot of your hours. Keep the tasks that need your judgement: pricing, key customer relationships, quality checks and money decisions. Your owner-hours number from your dashboard shows where your time goes.
Handing over a task
List weekly tasks and hours
Pick a repeatable task
Write a task card
Train, watch and check
Hand over fully
Delegation works when the standard is written and checked, not just explained once.
Worked example: Blessing hands over ironing

For example, Blessing's laundry now handles about 300 items a month. She irons everything herself at about 6 minutes per item. A helper would be paid about ₦100 per item ironed (approximate, for illustration).
Time spent ironing: 300 items × 6 minutes = 1,800 minutes = 30 hours a month.
Cost of a helper: 300 × ₦100 = ₦30,000 a month.
Blessing uses the freed 30 hours to visit offices and sign 2 office contracts for weekly pickup.
Each office contract brings about ₦25,000 extra profit a month: 2 × ₦25,000 = ₦50,000.
Net gain: ₦50,000 − ₦30,000 = ₦20,000 more profit a month, plus a stronger business.

Delegating ironing pays because Blessing uses her freed time on work only she can do: winning and keeping bigger customers. Delegating without a plan for the freed hours would simply have cost her ₦30,000.
A task card and a simple agreement
**Task card**: the task name, the steps, what "done well" looks like, the safety rules and who to call with problems.
**Work agreement**: tasks, hours or pay per item, pay day, trial period, notice period, and rules on customer data and money.
Read the agreement together, give a copy, and keep one yourself; a WhatsApp message both of you reply to is better than nothing.

A referral partner may ask for a small commission, often agreed as a percentage of each order; write it down and pay it promptly to keep trust.

After any partnership conversation, send a short message: "Thank you for today. To confirm: you will refer party clients to me, and I will pay 5 percent of each order you send, by transfer within 3 days of payment. Please reply OK if correct." This avoids misunderstandings later.

For example, Aisha and four other food sellers in her area each use about 2 kegs of vegetable oil a month. Prices are approximate and for illustration.

As your team and partners grow, communication becomes part of your job. Hold a short weekly check-in with helpers: what went well, what went wrong, what changes next week. Praise good work specifically. Correct mistakes privately and calmly, with reference to the task card. When you meet other women in business, share what you have learned; strong networks lift everyone in them.

Your 90-day growth plan and final project
Turn your growth move into one SMART 90-day goal
Break the goal into monthly targets and weekly actions
Choose leading and result measures to track
Assemble your final project from the work done in this course

Ninety days is long enough to see real results and short enough to stay focused. In this final lesson you bring everything together: your diagnosis, customer profile, canvas, costing, standards, dashboard, growth move and partnerships, into one plan you can follow on your phone or in a notebook.
Write one SMART goal

A SMART goal is **Specific** (what exactly), **Measurable** (a number), **Achievable** (stretching but realistic for your resources), **Relevant** (it fixes your main limit) and **Time-bound** (a date). "Grow my business" is not a goal. "Increase monthly items processed from 300 to 420 by 31 March, with a complaint rate under 1.5 percent" is.
Leading and result measures

A **result measure** shows whether you reached the goal, for example items processed or monthly profit. A **leading measure** is an action you control that drives the result, for example office visits made each week or follow-up messages sent. Track both: leading measures warn you early if you are falling behind.
The 90-day plan in four phases
Days 1-14: prepare
Days 15-45: launch
Days 46-75: adjust
Days 76-90: review
Prepare tools and people first, launch, adjust using your numbers, then review honestly.
Worked example: Blessing's 90-day plan
For example, Blessing's main limit is time, and her customer profile shows that office workers value reliable pickup. Her growth move is office contracts plus a helper for ironing.
Goal: increase items processed from 300 to 420 a month within 90 days, with a complaint rate under 1.5 percent.
Monthly targets: 340 items in Month 1, 380 in Month 2, 420 in Month 3, an increase of 40 items each month.
Days 1 to 14: recruit and train the ironing helper with a task card; print simple price cards for offices.
Days 15 to 45: visit 3 offices a week (leading measure) and offer a weekly pickup day.
Days 46 to 75: check the dashboard; if fewer than 2 offices have signed, ask receptionists who else to contact and ask current customers for referrals.
Days 76 to 90: compare all six dashboard numbers with the starting month and decide the next 90-day goal.
Each week Blessing knows exactly what to do and what to count. If items processed reach 420 with complaints under 1.5 percent, that is 6 complaints or fewer (420 × 1.5 ÷ 100 = 6.3), the goal is met.
A person standing beside a target with an arrow in the centre
One clear goal with weekly actions turns a growth idea into results.
Risks and a weekly rhythm
Write the two biggest risks to your plan (for example, the helper leaves, or input prices rise) and one response for each.
Set one fixed weekly slot, such as Sunday evening for 30 minutes, to update your leading measures.
At the end of each month, update the dashboard and write one action.
Tell one trusted person, such as a mentor or a fellow member of your network, about your goal and agree to report progress to them.

If you fall behind

Most plans fall behind somewhere. If your leading measure is on track but the result is not, your actions may be the wrong ones: go back to your customers and ask why. If the leading measure itself is behind, the problem is time or discipline: shrink the weekly action until you can do it every week. Change the plan on purpose, write the change down, and keep going. Abandoning a plan quietly is the most common way growth stops.
Using your plan with lenders and partners

Your final project is also a document you can show. A cooperative, microfinance bank or mentor will take you more seriously when you can show three months of dashboard numbers, a costed growth move with its payback period, and a plan for repaying any loan from extra profit. Keep a clean copy in a folder or a phone album, and update it every 90 days.

When the 90 days end, celebrate what worked, even if you did not reach the full target. Then start the next cycle: update your stage diagnosis, readiness score and canvas, compare them with your first versions from Module 1, and choose the next limit to fix. Steady 90-day cycles, repeated over a year, are how a stable business becomes a growing one.
Be honest in your project

Use your real numbers, marked as estimates where needed. A plan built on honest figures is far more useful to you, and to any lender, cooperative or mentor who reads it, than one that looks impressive but cannot be checked.

Cash: you cannot buy inputs in advance
Time: you are the bottleneck for every task
Each business has a main limit, and each limit needs a different fix. Demand means not enough people are buying.
Capacity means you cannot make or deliver more. That is Aisha. Customers already want more than one fryer can make.
Cash means you cannot buy stock or inputs in advance.
Time means every task waits for you. The fix is delegation and routines.
If your profit per hour is lower than a helper would cost, the business is quietly using your free labour. That is not failure. It is information.
Customer discovery
Weak question
Would you pay 1,500 naira for this?
Strong question
The last time you used a laundry?
What did you spend on this last month?
Have you told anyone about us?
Next, find out who really buys. People are polite. If you ask whether they would buy, most say yes and never buy.
So ask about what they actually did recently. Past behaviour is the best evidence of future behaviour.
Step by step
Ask permission before you save a number or quote anyone.
Talk to best, lost and competitors' customers
Aim for 10 to 15 talks of about 10 minutes
Ask about past behaviour; do not pitch
Write notes the same day, then tally
Write one paragraph: who, problem, why you
Talk to your best regular customers, customers who stopped buying, and people who buy from a competitor. Each group tells you something different.
Aim for 10 to 15 short conversations.
Ask what happened the last time they bought, what was hardest, and why they chose you. Do not pitch or defend.
Write notes the same day and tally the answers that repeat. Blessing, who runs a laundry in Port Harcourt, found 7 of 12 people said late return was their biggest frustration. Only 2 mentioned price.
So her growth idea changed from cut prices to a 48-hour return with office pickup. Your profile names who buys, their problem, why they choose you, and why they leave.
One rule. Ask permission before you save a phone number or quote anyone, and never share customers' numbers or chats.
Readiness check
Score yourself honestly
Now put the whole business on one page with the Business Model Canvas. Circle the two weakest blocks.
Then score the ten readiness statements, from 0 for not true to 2 for fully true. Here are five of them.
Titi, who keeps hens near Ibadan, scored 11 out of 20. Her lowest areas were no customer profile and no cash reserve.
Under 8, fix records and separate money first. From 8 to 14, fix your two lowest items. 15 and above, you are probably ready to plan growth.
Remember

Name your main limit: demand, capacity, cash or time
Ask what people did, not what they might do
Your readiness score shows your two urgent fixes
Remember. Growth spent at survival stage leaks into the household. Profit is sales minus all costs, and dividing it by your hours shows if the business pays you fairly.

Module 2 video
Quote orders properly, keep quality steady, track six numbers
Quote orders properly, keep quality steady, and track six numbers.
This is the video for module two of Women Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development.
Why this matters
Turn good intentions into routines
Cost and quote a full order without losing money
Write a quality standard a helper can follow
Keep your business, helpers and customers safe
Track six numbers every month
Growing businesses sell by order: a party tray, a set of uniforms, crates of eggs for a hotel. If you quote from habit, a big order can make you busy and poorer at the same time.
As soon as a helper joins, quality depends on a standard that is written down and checked.
Growth also brings more gas, more power and more money moving, so safety matters more.
And a monthly dashboard replaces the feeling that business is okay with real numbers.
Costing an order
Direct inputs: everything in the product
Packaging: packs, bags, labels, crates
Shared running costs: gas, power, fuel
Delivery, including the return trip
Labour: helpers plus your own hours
Payment costs: gateway, POS and transfer fees
Every order has six cost lines. First, direct inputs: ingredients, fabric, feed or detergent.
Second, packaging.
Third, the order's fair share of gas, electricity or generator fuel.
Fourth, delivery, and remember the return trip.
Fifth, labour. That includes your own hours at a fair rate you decide, for example 1,000 naira per hour.
Sixth, payment fees, usually a percentage of the price. Your own time and these fees are the two lines owners forget most.
Worked example
Aisha costs 50 party packs
For example, a client in Kaduna asks Aisha for 50 small chops packs for a birthday.
Naira prices are approximate.
Here is a worked example. The client will pay through a payment link.
Ingredients cost 38,500 naira. Packaging is 50 packs at 250 naira each, so 12,500.
Gas, delivery and a helper for the day add 14,000. Her own 10 hours at 1,000 naira add 10,000.
Total cost, 75,000 naira. That is 1,500 naira per pack.
From cost to quote
Quote it, then protect your cash
Confirm payment in your own app, never by SMS or screenshot.
Price = cost ÷ (1 minus margin minus fee rate)
Round sensibly and check the profit
Take a deposit that covers what you must buy
Put the terms in writing, even on WhatsApp
Margin is profit as a share of the price. Aisha wants 25 percent, and the link fee is 1.5 percent. So 75,000 divided by 0.735 gives about 102,041 naira.
She rounds to 2,050 naira a pack, 102,500 in total. Had she quoted 1,800 a pack from habit, her profit would be about 13,650 naira, roughly half, for the same work.
Her ingredients and packaging cost 51,000, so a 50 percent deposit of 51,250 covers them.
Write the quantity, price, delivery date, deposit, when the balance is due, and what happens if the client cancels late.
And never release goods because of an SMS or a screenshot. Scammers send convincing fake credit alerts, especially on large orders. Check inside your own bank or wallet app.
Quality standard
Quality without and with a standard
Without a written standard, quality depends on mood, and the same complaints come back.
Write your steps on one page, with a check anyone can do: a time, a weight, a count. Then track your complaint rate: complaints divided by orders, times 100.
Blessing tagged every laundry bag and counted items in and out. Her rate fell from 2.5 percent to 1 percent while volume rose.
Safety first
Safety basics as you grow
Keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep safe temperatures, use safe water.
Ventilate, check hoses with soapy water, never leave hot oil, do not overload sockets.
Always outside, away from doors, windows and vents. Exhaust fumes have no smell and can kill.
For food, follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep safe temperatures, and use safe water.
With gas, cook in a ventilated space, check hoses for leaks with soapy water, and keep a fire blanket or extinguisher nearby. Do not overload sockets, and keep irons away from water.
Run a generator outside, well away from doors and windows. Its exhaust has no smell and can kill people sleeping or working nearby.
Monthly dashboard
Six numbers, every month
Revenue
Gross margin
Net profit
Cash at month end
Repeat customer rate
Owner hours
Write the same six numbers each month: revenue, gross margin, net profit, cash at month end, repeat customer rate, and your own hours.
Watch profit and cash side by side. Titi's egg profit rose to 105,000 naira in Month 3, but a hotel still owed her 180,000 for eggs on credit, so her cash fell.
Many profitable small businesses close because they run out of cash. End every review with one written action.
Remember

Take a deposit and confirm payments in your own app
Write a quality standard and track complaints
Track six numbers and choose one action monthly
Remember. Count all six cost lines. Use the margin formula, take a deposit, and confirm every payment in your own app.
Write your standard so a helper can follow it, and track six numbers every month.

This is the video for module three of Women Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development.
Why this matters
Growth means more profit, not more stress
Choose one growth move that fixes your main limit
Test if a loan is affordable, even in a slow month
Hand over tasks and find partners
Write a 90-day plan you can follow
Growth does not always mean a bigger shop or a big loan. It means more profit from a business that still runs well. You will choose one move that fixes your main limit.
You will test whether borrowing is safe.
You will hand over tasks so the business does not depend on you for everything.
And you will write a 90-day plan, which becomes your final project.
Growth moves
Sell more to existing customers
Reach new customers like your best ones
Raise the price where quality justifies it
Add capacity: equipment, a helper, a process
Add a product customers already ask for
Sell more to existing customers, with bigger packs, subscriptions or reminders before festive seasons.
Use your customer profile to find more people like your best buyers.
Raise the price. If Titi moves from 5,500 to 5,800 naira a crate, at 150 crates a month that is 45,000 naira more profit with no new equipment.
Add capacity so you can say yes to more orders.
Or add what the same customers already ask for. Many owners jump to a big bet, like a second shop, before trying these quick wins.
Worked example
Can Aisha afford a second fryer?
For example, Aisha refuses about 3 party orders a month because she has only one fryer.
Second fryer and burner
Extra profit each month
Loan repayment each month
Naira prices are approximate.
Every investment needs a payback period: its cost divided by the extra monthly profit it brings. A short payback is lower risk.
A second fryer and gas burner cost about 180,000 naira.
3 extra orders at 20,000 naira profit each bring 60,000 a month. So the payback is 3 months.
A loan repaid at 36,000 a month for 6 months means she repays 216,000. The loan costs 36,000.
That leaves 24,000 a month. Now the bad-month test. If only 2 extra orders come, just 4,000 is left after repayment.
So Aisha takes a cooperative loan for half and uses savings for the rest. A slow month will not break her.
Money safety
Climb the funding ladder, safest first
Never pay a fee to receive a grant.
Thrift groups and cooperatives you know
Microfinance: get the total cost in writing
Loan apps: FCCPC-approved, emergencies only
Grants: check official websites only
Start with your own retained profit and savings. It is slower, but there is no debt.
Join ajo, esusu, adashe or cooperatives only with people you know and clear written rules.
Ask a microfinance bank to write down the amount you receive, every fee, the total you repay and the dates. Compare the repayment with the extra profit, not your total sales.
Use loan apps only for short emergencies, only if they are on the FCCPC list of approved digital lenders, and avoid apps that demand your contacts.
Genuine grants never ask for a processing fee to a person's account. Confirm SMEDAN or Bank of Industry programmes only on their official websites.
Delegation
What to hand over, what to keep
Hand over
Repeatable tasks
Easy to check
Take many of your hours
Keep
Pricing
Key customer relationships
Quality checks and money decisions
Delegate tasks that are repeatable, easy to check and take a lot of your hours. Use a written task card and a simple work agreement.

Keep pricing, key customers, quality checks and money. Blessing paid a helper 30,000 naira a month for ironing and used the freed 30 hours to win 2 office contracts worth 50,000. Without that plan, delegating would only have cost her.
Your 90-day plan
Four phases in 90 days
Write one SMART goal that fixes your limit
Days 1 to 14: prepare tools and people
Days 15 to 45: launch
Days 46 to 75: adjust using your numbers
Days 76 to 90: review honestly
A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Blessing's: grow from 300 to 420 items a month in 90 days, with complaints under 1.5 percent.
Prepare first. She trains the ironing helper with a task card.
Launch. She visits 3 offices a week. That is her leading measure, an action she controls that drives the result.
Adjust. If fewer than 2 offices have signed, she asks receptionists and customers for referrals.
Review. Compare all six dashboard numbers with the starting month, then set the next goal.
Remember
What to keep from this module
Try quick wins before big bets
Payback = cost ÷ extra monthly profit
A loan must pass the bad-month test
Delegate only with a plan for the freed hours
Track a leading measure every week
Remember. Try quick wins before big bets. Work out the payback period, and borrow only if the loan passes the bad-month test.
If you fall behind, change the plan on purpose and write it down. Abandoning a plan quietly is the most common way growth stops.
